Trends and disparities in stroke mortality with diabetes as a contributing cause among U.S. adults, 1999–2023: a uniform-definition national analysis of long-term decline and a post-2014, pandemic-era increase

Abstract

Background

Diabetes mellitus is a major contributor to cerebrovascular risk and stroke-related mortality. Although U.S. cardiovascular mortality declined for decades, national estimates for stroke mortality among people with diabetes have been inconsistent, partly because of differences in case definition and in the handling of the 2018 change in population race classification.

Methods

Using the CDC WONDER Multiple Cause of Death database, we studied U.S. adults aged ≥ 25 years (1999–2023) under a single, frozen case definition: stroke as the underlying cause (ICD-10 I60–I69) with diabetes mellitus (E10–E14) contributing. Age-adjusted mortality rates (AAMRs; 2000 U.S. standard) were analysed with segmented log-linear regression. Sensitivity analyses excluded the 2020–2021 pandemic peak, tested a 2020 level shift, applied inverse-variance weighting and age-specific count models, denominated the rate by NHANES diabetes prevalence, and examined proportional mortality; subgroup change points were bootstrapped.

Results

Among 298,908 stroke deaths with contributing diabetes, the national AAMR declined from 1999 to 2014 (APC − 3.97%; 95% CI − 4.38 to − 3.56) and then rose through 2023 (+ 3.19%; +2.40 to + 3.99), from 4.28 to 5.37 per 100,000. The increase was concentrated in the pandemic era: the strictly pre-pandemic segment (2014–2019) was not significant (+ 0.55%, P = 0.31; +0.73% in an age-specific count model), a 2020 level shift fit best, and the rise persisted after excluding 2020–2021 (+ 2.88%). It was not accounted for by rising diabetes prevalence (rate per adult with diabetes + 2.92%; age-adjusted prevalence flat), although increasing diabetes ascertainment on death certificates could not be excluded. The non-Hispanic Black: White rate ratio was roughly stable (≈ 2.0), while the absolute gap re-widened (9.37 vs. 4.71 per 100,000 in 2023). The increase was broad but heterogeneous, with the largest point estimate in the South and no increase in the Northeast.

Conclusions

After a long decline, stroke mortality among adults with diabetes stopped falling around 2014 and increased modestly in the pandemic era. This increase was not accounted for by rising diabetes prevalence, although increasing diabetes ascertainment could not be excluded, and the rate remained above the 2014 nadir. These findings underscore continued surveillance and life-course prevention, with the greatest burden among non-Hispanic Black adults and in the South.

Keywords: Stroke, Diabetes mellitus, Mortality, Temporal trends, Health disparities, CDC WONDER

Introduction

Stroke remains a leading cause of mortality and long-term disability in the United States despite substantial declines in age-adjusted death rates during the early 21st century [1, 2]. These improvements have been attributed to advances in acute stroke care, expanded use of antihypertensive and lipid-lowering therapies, and reductions in smoking [1–3]. However, recent national reports suggest that progress in cardiovascular and cerebrovascular mortality reduction may have stalled or reversed in some subpopulations [4, 5].

Diabetes mellitus is a major contributor to cerebrovascular risk and stroke-related mortality, operating through chronic inflammation, endothelial dysfunction and accelerated atherosclerosis [6, 7]. The prevalence of diagnosed diabetes among U.S. adults has risen over two decades, in parallel with obesity, particularly among middle-aged populations [8, 9]. People with diabetes experience substantially higher stroke incidence and case fatality than those without, underscoring the importance of accurately monitoring stroke mortality in this high-risk group [6, 10].

Studies of stroke mortality among people with diabetes have reported heterogeneous trends [11, 12]. These discrepancies may reflect differences in case definition, analytic time windows, and the handling of administrative changes in national data. Two issues are particularly relevant. First, studies vary in whether stroke is defined by the underlying versus any listed (multiple) cause of death, which can substantially change observed patterns [6, 13]. Second, in 2018 the National Center for Health Statistics transitioned population estimates from bridged-race to single-race classification, introducing a change in rate denominators (especially for race-specific estimates) that must be handled consistently in analyses spanning that year [14]. Notably, a change in the classification of race is not expected to move the all-race (aggregate) trend materially, because reallocation among race groups nets out in aggregate; its principal effect is on race-stratified comparability across 2018.

The objective of this study was to provide an updated national assessment of long-term trends in stroke mortality among U.S. adults with comorbid diabetes from 1999 to 2023, using a single uniform case definition applied consistently across the study period, and to characterise disparities by sex, race/ethnicity, census region and age. By extending analyses through 2023 and testing whether recent changes persisted after excluding the 2020–2021 pandemic-peak years, this study aims to provide a reproducible characterisation of the evolving burden of stroke–diabetes comorbidity.

Methods

Data source and study population

This retrospective population-based study used national mortality data from the CDC WONDER Multiple Cause of Death database. We included all deaths in the 50 states and the District of Columbia among adults aged ≥ 25 years from 1 January 1999 through 31 December 2023. The ≥ 25-year restriction minimises misclassification related to childhood stroke and rare diabetes subtypes and was applied uniformly to every extraction. Population denominators were obtained directly from CDC WONDER.

Case definition (uniform across the study period)

A single, frozen case definition was applied to all national and subgroup extractions. Stroke was defined as the underlying cause of death (ICD-10 I60–I69), and diabetes mellitus (E10–E14) was required to appear as a contributing (multiple) cause. This definition prioritises deaths in which a cerebrovascular event was the primary terminal cause in the context of established diabetes, and it was verified against the query criteria recorded at the bottom of every data export to ensure that the underlying-cause and age restrictions were applied identically in all files.

Data-system harmonisation across 1999–2023

Because no single CDC WONDER dataset spans the full period, two datasets were combined: the bridged-race Multiple Cause of Death file (1999–2020) and the single-race file (2018–2024). To span 1999–2023, the bridged-race file provided 1999–2020 and the single-race file provided 2021–2023. In the overlapping years (2018–2020) the two datasets agreed closely for the all-race aggregate, returning age-adjusted rates identical to two decimal places under the uniform definition (e.g., 4.42 per 100,000 in 2018 under both), confirming that the series can be joined without discontinuity and that a comparability adjustment is not required for the all-race aggregate.

Race and ethnicity were classified as non-Hispanic White, non-Hispanic Black and Hispanic, which are comparable across the study period. The bridged-race (four-category) and single-race (six-category) schemes are not directly comparable for other groups; American Indian/Alaska Native and Asian/Pacific Islander populations were therefore analysed in a segmented manner (1999–2020 under the bridged-race scheme; 2018–2023 under the single-race scheme), and Native Hawaiian/Other Pacific Islander and multiple-race categories (available only from 2018 and with small counts) were reported for 2018–2023 only (Supplementary Material). Sex, seven 10-year age groups (25–34 to ≥ 85 years) and four census regions were analysed with the same uniform definition.

Statistical analysis

AAMRs were calculated per 100,000 using direct standardisation to the 2000 U.S. standard population. Because CDC WONDER does not produce age-adjusted rates when data are grouped by age, age-specific analyses used age-specific crude rates. Temporal trends were analysed with segmented log-linear regression incorporating a single data-selected change point, a segmented-regression approach [15] related to joinpoint trend models [16]. For each series the log mortality rate was regressed on calendar year, and the change-point year was selected by minimising the residual sum of squares over all feasible change points leaving at least five observations in each segment (2003–2019); because the data are annual, the change point was constrained to a calendar year. Segment annual percentage changes (APCs; APC = exp(bi) − 1 for segment slope bi) and the full-period average annual percentage change (AAPC = exp(Σi wi bi) − 1, where wi is the length of segment i as a fraction of the study period) were derived from the fitted model. Confidence intervals used t-distribution critical values (degrees of freedom = n − number of model parameters); the variance of the AAPC and of the recent (combined) slope was obtained from the full covariance matrix of the segment slopes, explicitly including their pairwise covariances. Two-sided tests used P < 0.05. A prespecified sensitivity analysis re-estimated the recent segment after excluding the 2020–2021 pandemic-peak years while holding the change point fixed. The change point was selected independently for the overall population and each subgroup. Because the analytic confidence intervals are conditional on the selected change point, we additionally re-selected the change point within a nonparametric residual bootstrap (3000 resamples): for the overall series the change point fell at 2014 in 72% of resamples and the recent-segment bootstrap 95% CI (+ 2.18% to + 4.43%) was only modestly wider than the analytic interval, and the selected change point and segment estimates were unchanged across candidate windows from 2003 to 2019 to 2011–2018. This approach is fully reproducible from the observed rates; it does not employ the Monte Carlo permutation selection of the Joinpoint Regression Program, and the results are reported accordingly. As an independent check using established software, the overall and all subgroup series were re-fitted with the R segmented package [15], which estimates the change point as a continuous parameter and formally tests its existence (Davies test); this reproduced the findings: an overall change point of 2014.4 (Davies P < 0.001), with concordant direction and statistical significance across subgroups and recent-segment APCs differing from the primary estimates by at most 0.7% points.

The national aggregate and all continuously-comparable subgroup trends were estimated on directly obtained observed rates without a jump term. For the race-stratified series, which cross the 2018 bridged-to-single-race boundary, we compared the two schemes in the overlapping years 2018–2020: non-Hispanic White rates were essentially identical (single-race/bridged ratio ≈ 1.00), whereas non-Hispanic Black single-race rates were about 1.5% higher than bridged (ratio ≈ 1.015). The main analysis used bridged rates through 2020 and single-race rates from 2021 without a jump term; sensitivity analyses that instead placed the splice at 2018 or rescaled the single-race series to the bridged scale changed the non-Hispanic Black recent-segment APC only marginally (from + 4.54% to between + 4.32% and + 4.58%, all P < 0.001; Supplementary Material), so this small discontinuity does not affect the conclusions. A prespecified sensitivity analysis excluding the 2020–2021 pandemic-peak years was performed for the overall series and every subgroup to determine whether the post-2014 increase persisted.

Robustness and specification

Several sensitivity analyses were performed for the overall series: inverse-variance–weighted models; age-specific Poisson and negative-binomial models with age-group fixed effects and a population offset (a quasi-Poisson scale was used where overdispersion was present); assessment of residual autocorrelation (Durbin–Watson) with Newey–West standard errors; and, to separate a pre-existing trend from a pandemic shift, refitting the recent segment excluding 2020–2021 and fitting a level-plus-slope change model at 2020 (compared with the slope-only model by AIC). For every subgroup the recent segment was additionally refitted at the common national 2014 change point for like-for-like comparison, and change-point stability was quantified by a parametric bootstrap (2000 resamples; each annual log-rate resampled by its standard error and the change point re-selected), reporting the modal change point and its selection frequency.

Denominator and reporting-drift analyses

Because the AAMR denominator is the whole adult population, two further analyses were performed. To test whether rising diabetes prevalence could account for the trend, the rate was re-expressed per 100,000 adults with diagnosed diabetes by dividing the AAMR by NHANES age-adjusted diagnosed-diabetes prevalence; this is an ecological approximation (age-adjusted numerator; ages ≥ 25 vs. ≥ 20; two-year survey cycles interpolated). To assess reporting drift, two proportional-mortality series were computed from additional extractions (stroke-with-diabetes deaths as a proportion of all stroke deaths, and any-mention-of-diabetes deaths as a proportion of all deaths), both using death counts only and therefore independent of the bridged-to-single-race population transition. Suppressed cells (counts < 10) were dropped rather than imputed.

Results

Overall national trends

Between 1999 and 2023, 298,908 deaths were identified in which stroke was the underlying cause and diabetes a contributing cause (Table 1). The national AAMR declined steadily from 1999 to a nadir of 4.28 per 100,000 in 2014 (Fig. 1). A segmented log-linear model placed the change point at 2014: the rate fell significantly from 1999 to 2014 (APC − 3.97%; 95% CI − 4.38 to − 3.56; P < 0.001) and then rose from 2014 to 2023 (APC + 3.19%; 95% CI + 2.40 to + 3.99; P < 0.001), reaching 5.37 per 100,000 in 2023, about 25% above the nadir. Excluding the 2020–2021 pandemic-peak years, the 2014–2023 increase remained significant (APC + 2.88%; 95% CI + 1.29 to + 4.50). The increase was, however, concentrated in the pandemic era: in the strictly pre-pandemic window (2014–2019) the trend was not significant in the aggregate rate model (APC + 0.55%; 95% CI − 0.75 to + 1.86; P = 0.31), though a more powerful age-specific count model gave a small significant slope (+ 0.73%; 95% CI + 0.14 to + 1.33; P = 0.02). A model allowing a level shift at 2020 fit substantially better than a slope-only model (ΔAIC ≈ 11), with a significant step (+ 19.5%; P = 0.003) and no significant residual post-2014 slope; conversely, the elevation did not return to baseline, the 2023 rate remaining well above the 2014 nadir. Findings were unchanged under inverse-variance weighting and under quasi-Poisson and negative-binomial count models, and the recent increase remained significant with autocorrelation-robust (Newey–West) inference (Durbin–Watson 1.20; recent APC + 3.32%, 95% CI + 2.35 to + 4.30). The full-period AAPC (1999–2023) was − 1.34% (95% CI − 1.59 to − 1.09), reflecting the net long decline; given the fall-then-rise shape we emphasise the segment-specific APCs (Table 2).

Rate per adult with diabetes

To test whether rising diabetes prevalence could account for the increase, the rate was re-expressed per 100,000 adults with diagnosed diabetes using NHANES age-adjusted prevalence, which was essentially flat after 2015 (10.0% in 2015–2016, 10.6% in 2017–2020, 10.1% in 2021–2023; APC + 0.38%, not significant). On this denominator the increase persisted (2014–2023 APC + 2.92%; 95% CI + 1.27 to + 4.61; P = 0.008; excluding 2020–2021 + 2.54%; P = 0.03), essentially unchanged from the population rate. Rising diabetes prevalence therefore accounts for at most about 0.4% points of the ≈ 3%/year increase (Supplementary Material). This is an ecological approximation and is interpreted with corresponding caution.

Proportional mortality

Two proportional-mortality series were examined. Stroke-with-diabetes deaths as a share of all stroke deaths were flat before the change point (1999–2014 APC + 0.04%; P = 0.77) and then rose (2014–2023 + 2.70%; P < 0.001; excluding 2020–2021 + 2.50%; P = 0.002). Any-mention-of-diabetes deaths as a share of all deaths rose at a very similar rate (2014–2023 + 2.62%; P = 0.001). The ratio of these two proportions (an index of whether diabetes was recorded increasingly on stroke death certificates beyond the general trend) did not change after 2014 (APC + 0.08%; 95% CI − 0.56 to + 0.73; P = 0.81). The rise in diabetes co-listing among stroke deaths therefore tracked the general increase in diabetes reporting on death certificates rather than being stroke-specific, so these proportional analyses cannot exclude increasing diabetes ascertainment as a contributor to the observed increase (Supplementary Material).

Sex-specific trends

Men had higher rates than women throughout (2023: 6.07 vs. 4.85 per 100,000; men approximately 25% higher). Both sexes declined until the mid-2010s and then rose significantly. Both sexes rose significantly after the change point, with similar recent slopes and overlapping confidence intervals (men + 3.59%, 95% CI + 2.80 to + 4.39; women + 3.72%, 95% CI + 2.78 to + 4.67); men had higher absolute rates, but the point estimates do not support a steeper increase in either sex, and no formal interaction was tested. Both segments remained significant after excluding 2020–2021 (men + 3.15%; women + 2.99%) (Fig. 2A; Table 2).

Racial and ethnic disparities

Non-Hispanic Black adults consistently had the highest burden (Fig. 2). All three groups declined before the mid-2010s and rose thereafter, with significant recent increases that persisted after excluding 2020–2021 (non-Hispanic Black + 3.64%; non-Hispanic White + 3.13%; Hispanic + 2.44%; all P < 0.05). The non-Hispanic Black: White age-adjusted rate ratio was roughly stable over time, at 2.16 (95% CI 2.06–2.26) in 1999, 2.10 (1.99–2.21) in 2014 and 1.99 (1.90–2.08) in 2023, so the relative gap did not widen; the absolute gap narrowed during the decline (from 7.70 per 100,000 in 1999 to 3.79 in 2019) and then re-widened in the pandemic era (to 4.66 in 2023; non-Hispanic Black 9.37 vs. non-Hispanic White 4.71). American Indian/Alaska Native and Asian populations, not comparable across the 2018 classification change, are reported separately (Supplementary Material); for the more-than-one-race category, which exists only from 2018, we report counts rather than a percentage change (stroke-with-diabetes deaths 43, 43, 55, 55, 81 and 94 in 2018–2023).

Regional variation

The South had the highest rates throughout, and the largest recent-segment APC point estimate among regions (2023: 6.44 per 100,000; recent APC + 5.20% overall and + 4.61% excluding 2020–2021; both P < 0.05); between-region differences were not formally tested and are described descriptively. The West (+ 2.99%) and Midwest (+ 1.72%) also rose significantly after excluding the pandemic peak. The Northeast, by contrast, did not participate in the recent increase. Under its data-selected change point (2010) its recent trend was a modest decline (− 0.71%; 95% CI − 1.24 to − 0.17), but this estimate is fragile: in a change-point bootstrap the 2010 change point was selected in only 35% of resamples, and when the Northeast was refitted at the common national 2014 change point its recent trend was not significant (+ 0.40%; 95% CI − 0.77 to + 1.58; P = 0.51). What is robust is that the Northeast, unlike other regions, showed no recent increase; its strictly pre-pandemic 2014–2019 trend was a significant decline (− 1.87%; P = 0.02) (Fig. 2; Table 2).

Age-specific trends

Absolute rates rose steeply with age (2023 crude rates: 68.93 per 100,000 at ≥ 85 years vs. 1.24 at 45–54 years). All age groups ≥ 45 years showed significant recent increases that persisted after excluding 2020–2021, including middle-aged adults (45–54 years + 4.61%; 55–64 years + 4.12%) and older adults (65–74 + 2.56%; 75–84 + 2.05%; ≥85 + 3.92%; all P < 0.05). Rates in adults aged 25–44 years were very low and did not change significantly (Fig. 2; Table 2). Because the open-ended ≥ 85-year group’s internal age composition shifted over 1999–2023, its crude-rate trend should be read with corresponding caution. The pronounced relative increase in midlife is notable in light of prior reports of increasing stroke incidence among younger adults [17].

Discussion

Principal findings

In this national analysis, stroke mortality among U.S. adults with comorbid diabetes declined for more than a decade and then stopped falling around 2014, rising through 2023. The magnitude of the increase was modest (about + 3% per year; roughly 25% above the 2014 nadir) and remained significant after excluding the 2020–2021 pandemic-peak years, but it was concentrated in the pandemic era: the strictly pre-pandemic 2014–2019 slope was not significant in the aggregate rate model (though marginally so in a count model), and a level shift at 2020 fit the data better than a continuous post-2014 slope. Two interpretations are consistent with these data and cannot be distinguished here: a small pre-existing inflection in the mid-2010s that was amplified by the pandemic, or a pandemic-era level shift that has not returned to baseline. Under either reading, the long decline has halted and the 2023 rate remained above the 2014 nadir. We retained the segmented model as the primary descriptive analysis because it characterises the full 1999–2023 trajectory, whereas the 2020 level-shift model was used specifically to assess whether the shape of the recent elevation was better represented by a pandemic-era discontinuity. The change was broad but heterogeneous, present in both sexes, most regions and all age groups ≥ 45 years, with the Northeast a clear exception; the greatest burden remained among non-Hispanic Black adults, in the South, and among older adults.

Comparison with prior studies

These findings are best understood alongside a recent CDC WONDER analysis of the same comorbidity over the same period [11], which used a broader, symmetric definition (stroke, I60–I64, or diabetes, each as an underlying or contributing cause) and reported a net long-term decline (average annual change − 2.32%), with the 2018–2021 rise described as a temporary pandemic reversal. The two studies are concordant on the long-term decline, the pandemic-era increase, and the subgroups bearing the greatest burden. They differ by design: our uniform definition requires stroke to be the underlying cause (I60–I69) with diabetes contributing, isolating fatal cerebrovascular events among people with diabetes (about half as many deaths, 13,276 vs. 29,045 in 1999). We additionally harmonise the two data systems, provide the full reproducible series, and show that under this definition the pandemic-era elevation had not returned to baseline by 2023 and is not accounted for by rising diabetes prevalence, although increasing diabetes ascertainment on death certificates could not be excluded. Our stricter, uniform-definition framing therefore isolates a more specific outcome and shows a post-2014 elevation that had not returned to baseline by 2023; the estimated magnitudes are smaller than, though directionally concordant with, that broader analysis. Whether stroke is defined by the underlying versus any listed cause, and whether the 1999–2020 and 2018–2023 systems are harmonised, can substantially alter the apparent magnitude of recent trends.

Possible contributing factors

Several non-mutually-exclusive factors may contribute to the halt and post-2014 increase, though none can be established from these ecological data. First, rising diabetes prevalence is an obvious candidate; however, because the age-adjusted prevalence of diagnosed diabetes changed little after 2015 and the increase persisted when the rate was denominated by the diabetic population, a compositional effect of rising prevalence cannot be the principal driver. Second, diabetes was increasingly recorded on death certificates over the period (any-mention-of-diabetes as a share of all deaths rose), and the rise in diabetes co-listing among stroke deaths tracked this general trend (the ratio of the two proportions did not change after 2014); increasing diabetes ascertainment therefore remains a plausible contributor that the present data cannot exclude, even though the prevalence-denominator analysis argues against rising diabetes prevalence as the explanation. Third, population-level improvements in cardiometabolic risk-factor control may have plateaued alongside rising obesity [8, 9]. Although glucose-lowering therapies with cardiovascular benefit (SGLT2 inhibitors and GLP-1 receptor agonists) were introduced over the past decade, their population-level uptake has been limited and unequal by race, ethnicity and socioeconomic status [18, 19], which may attenuate any population-level mortality benefit. Finally, the COVID-19 pandemic contributed to the 2020–2021 peak through direct vascular effects of SARS-CoV-2 [20, 21] and healthcare disruption [12]. These explanations are hypotheses for future work rather than established causes.

Limitations

Several limitations apply. First, and most importantly, spanning 1999–2023 requires combining two CDC WONDER data systems with different race-classification schemes and population-estimate methodologies; we addressed this by applying one uniform case definition throughout, verifying closely agreeing rates in overlapping years, and analysing non-comparable race groups separately, but residual differences across the transition cannot be entirely excluded (for non-Hispanic Black adults the single-race scheme yielded rates ~ 1.5% higher than bridged in overlapping years, a difference shown not to affect the trend estimates). We note that an inconsistency in case definition across data systems can, if unaddressed, substantially inflate apparent recent increases; the present analysis was designed specifically to avoid this. In addition, the change-point locations were data-selected, so the analytic confidence intervals are conditional on the selected change point; a bootstrap that re-selected the change point gave very similar intervals and confirmed that the overall change point (2014) was highly stable. Second, death-certificate data are subject to misclassification and underreporting, particularly for contributing conditions such as diabetes [13], and evolving certification and diabetes-ascertainment practices may have contributed to the observed increase; as the proportional-mortality analyses show, the present data cannot exclude this mechanism. Third, the ecological design precludes individual-level causal inference, and CDC WONDER lacks clinical detail (diabetes duration, glycaemic control, medications, obesity, smoking, socioeconomic status). Finally, ischaemic and haemorrhagic stroke subtypes were not distinguished; subtype-specific analyses are a priority for future work. Finally, the diabetes-prevalence denominator uses survey estimates on a different age basis and in two-year cycles and is therefore an approximation, and the crude-rate trend in the open-ended ≥ 85-year group may partly reflect shifts in its internal age structure.

Conclusions

After more than a decade of decline, stroke mortality among U.S. adults with diabetes stopped falling around 2014 and increased through 2023. The increase was of modest but real magnitude and persisted after excluding the 2020–2021 mortality peaks, but was concentrated in the pandemic era and not yet significant in the strictly pre-pandemic window; it was not accounted for by rising diabetes prevalence, although increasing diabetes ascertainment could not be excluded, and the 2023 rate remained above the 2014 nadir. The burden was broad but heterogeneous, greatest among non-Hispanic Black adults, in the South, and among older adults. Using a uniform case definition applied consistently across data systems, with the full annual series and query criteria provided for reproducibility, this analysis characterises these trends and underscores the importance of continued surveillance and life-course-oriented prevention for populations bearing disproportionate burden.
